  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Entrapment: Having no options, Old Memories: Old photos, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Vignette:
Clara was forty-one weeks into a routine that had always felt steady—her dental practice, her relationship with Mark, the quiet predictability of evenings at home—when a persistent cough and a low-grade fever refused to leave. She was a dentist, someone who spent her days bent over open mouths, her nose full of composite resin and eugenol, so at first she dismissed the fatigue as the tail end of a long flu season. But then her joints ached, her skin felt hot to the touch even when she was shivering, and one afternoon she looked down at her hands and saw a strange, lacy rash blooming across her forearms. The urgent care doctor sent her straight to the hospital. Within hours she was in isolation, a sepsis diagnosis that had already begun to affect her kidneys, and she remembers the moment the attending physician closed the curtain and said, very quietly, “We need to move fast.” What stayed with Clara was not the fear of death itself, but the sickening knowledge that she had no control—no options, no say, no way to walk out of that room. She lay in the narrow bed, tethered to IV lines, and understood that her body had become something separate from her will, something that could fail without asking permission.

She survived. The antibiotics worked, the infection cleared, and after three weeks she was discharged. But the world she came home to was not the same. The first time Mark handed her an old photo from their vacation the year before—her smiling, tanned, healthy—she felt such a hollow pang that she turned the frame face-down on the dresser and never picked it up again. The smell of antiseptic lingered everywhere: in the hand sanitizer at the grocery store, in the hallway of her own dental clinic, in the soap Mark used. Each time the odor hit her nostrils, her throat tightened and she felt the curtain closing around that bed again. She began to avoid things quietly, steadily, without fully naming it. She stopped examining her own body in the mirror; the sight of her reflection—the faint scars from the central line, the way her ribs seemed sharper—made her flinch. She started wearing long sleeves even in summer, not to hide scars but to avoid looking at her own arms. At work, she found herself pulling away from colleagues at lunch, making excuses to eat alone in her office. When a hygienist asked casually, “How are you feeling these days?” Clara gave a tight smile and said she was fine, then spent the rest of the afternoon rehearsing what she would have said if she had been honest.

The avoidance hardened into a routine. She stopped going to the gym because being around other people’s bodies felt unbearable. She avoided her own annual physical, canceling twice. She told Mark she didn’t want to talk about the hospital stay, not ever, and when he pressed gently she turned away and said she was just tired. Internally, Clara had come to believe that she was fundamentally weak—that other people went through worse and came out stronger, and that her inability to move past this proved something shameful. She was certain she had changed for the worse, that the Clara who had been confident and capable was gone, replaced by someone who flinched at her own heartbeat. Worst of all, she felt her body had betrayed her irrevocably; she could no longer trust its signals, its resilience, its basic promise of health. Every twinge, every ache, every tiny cough sent a current of alarm through her chest.

It was Mark who finally brought her to seek help. He told her, one evening after she had spent an hour sitting motionless on the sofa staring at a photo album she couldn’t bring herself to open, that he missed her, that the silence between them felt like a wall. Clara agreed to see a therapist because she was afraid of losing him, but also because she was exhausted by the constant vigilance—the way she scanned every hospital smell, every mirror, every old photograph for evidence of what she had become. She sat in the waiting room with her hands pressed flat against her thighs, trying not to breathe too deeply, and thought: *I just want to feel like myself again.* But she wasn’t sure that self existed anymore.

missing_explanations: The vignette does not provide an approximate age for Clara. The patient is reported as 39 years old, but the vignette only mentions 'forty-one weeks into a routine' which refers to time, not age.
